newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian economic growth may hit gold - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Asian economic growth may hit gold - analyst.

text.p: As Asian economies develop, the traditional reliance of populations on gold as a hedge against inflation is likely to decline, analyst Rhona O'Connell of London brokers T.Hoare and Co Ltd said on Wednesday.
But a drop in Asian demand may be prevented by an inherent social love of gold, she added.
"The inexorable process of industrialisation is a two-edged sword as far as the gold market is concerned," O'Connell said in an address to an Asia Gold Congress in Hong Kong.

Growing industrialisation in Asia markets should be cause for concern as other investment tools become available, but a passion for gold sustained over hundreds of years may reduce the threat to gold demand, she noted.
The demand picture in Asia was relatively mixed, she said.
In Malaysia and Thailand, for example, gold purchases have largely stabilised as people turn their attention to other consumer goods and to the equity markets for investment.
But Indonesia, where equity markets are volatile, and in India, where stock markets are plagued by scandals as well as volatility, gold still takes priority over other investments, she noted.
"What may suffer over time is bar hoarding, which is why it is important for the gold market that jewellery of high quality continue to be fabricated."
The so-called investing nations, the Middle East, the Indian Sub-Continent and the Far East including China, account for an average of 93 percent of the world's bar hoarding.

"As price volatility increases, unless there is a genuine local cause stemming from political or economic uncertainty, consumers tend to be frightened away from the market until calmer times prevail," O'Connell said.
